content: Pelvic organ prolapse (POP) is a medical condition predominantly affecting women, characterized by the descent or bulging of pelvic organs through the vaginal canal due to weakening of the pelvic floor muscles and connective tissues. The pelvic organs that may prolapse include the uterus, bladder (cystocele), rectum (rectocele), or small bowel (enterocele). The pathophysiology involves mechanical strain and connective tissue remodeling that compromise the support structures of the pelvis. POP is associated with risk factors such as childbirth trauma, aging, obesity, chronic cough, heavy lifting, and menopause-related estrogen deficiency. Symptoms can range from a sensation of vaginal bulging to urinary, bowel, or sexual dysfunction, although some cases are asymptomatic. Diagnosis commonly involves clinical pelvic examination supported by patient history and may incorporate imaging modalities like ultrasound or MRI for complex presentations. Management strategies vary by severity and patient preference, including conservative options such as pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT), pessary devices, and lifestyle modifications, or surgical repair for more pronounced or symptomatic cases. While anatomy-focused, treatment must consider functional outcomes and individual goals. Misconceptions include the belief that POP always requires surgery and that it inevitably worsens over time; however, many cases remain stable or improve with conservative care. Safety in management is paramount; for example, pessary use requires proper fitting and hygiene to prevent complications. Overall, understanding POP's multifactorial etiology and treatment continuum supports improved patient-centered care and quality of life.

chunk_title: Definition and Overview of Pelvic Organ Prolapse
content: Pelvic organ prolapse (POP) refers to the descent of pelvic organs into or through the vaginal canal due to loss of normal support. It involves structures including the uterus, bladder (cystocele), rectum (rectocele), and sometimes small intestine (enterocele). POP is classified by the organ involved and degree of descent. This condition predominantly affects adult and older women and can be asymptomatic or cause symptoms like vaginal bulge sensation, pelvic pressure, and urinary or bowel disturbances. Synonyms include genital prolapse and pelvic floor dysfunction (although the latter is broader). POP results from weakening of the pelvic floor muscles, ligaments, and connective tissue, which normally maintain pelvic organ position and function.

chunk_title: Anatomy and Physiology of the Pelvic Floor
content: The pelvic floor comprises muscles, ligaments, and connective tissue that form a supportive hammock at the base of the pelvis. Major muscles include the levator ani group (pubococcygeus, iliococcygeus, puborectalis). The endopelvic fascia and uterosacral ligaments provide critical connective tissue support. These structures maintain the position and function of pelvic organs, assist in continence, and contribute to sexual function. During activities like lifting or coughing, the pelvic floor counteracts intra-abdominal pressure, preventing descent of organs. Damage or weakening from childbirth, aging, or pressure overload compromises this support, predisposing to prolapse.

content: POP develops due to multifactorial causes that weaken pelvic support. Key risk factors include vaginal childbirth trauma causing muscle or nerve injury, aging-related tissue weakness, menopause-associated estrogen deficiency, chronic cough or constipation increasing intra-abdominal pressure, obesity, heavy physical labor or lifting, and prior pelvic surgeries. Genetic predisposition affecting connective tissue quality may also contribute. Parity (number of vaginal deliveries) is a strong risk factor, and the condition is more common in postmenopausal women. These factors cumulatively stress the pelvic floor beyond its capacity.

content: Symptoms vary depending on prolapse severity and organ involved. Common complaints include a feeling of vaginal fullness or bulge, pelvic pressure or heaviness, urinary symptoms (urgency, incontinence, difficulty emptying), bowel dysfunction (constipation, incomplete evacuation), and sexual dysfunction. Some women are asymptomatic and only diagnosed on examination. Symptoms typically worsen with standing, physical activity, or at the end of the day. The prolapse itself may be visible or palpable at the vaginal opening during Valsalva maneuver (straining).

content: Evaluation starts with detailed clinical history and pelvic physical examination, including inspection and palpation of the vaginal walls and uterus during rest and straining. The Pelvic Organ Prolapse Quantification (POP-Q) system is the standardized method to grade prolapse severity by measuring descent points relative to the hymen. Additional diagnostic tools include pelvic ultrasound and MRI to evaluate anatomical defects, especially in complex or recurrent cases. Urinary and bowel function assessments may accompany prolapse evaluation to guide treatment.

content: Initial management for mild to moderate POP focuses on conservative therapies. Pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT), also called Kegel exercises, strengthens pelvic muscles and improves support. Vaginal pessaries—removable devices inserted into the vagina—provide mechanical support and symptom relief. Lifestyle measures such as weight reduction, avoiding heavy lifting, managing constipation and cough, and smoking cessation reduce intra-abdominal pressure. These approaches can improve symptoms, delay progression, and are important first-line options especially for women who desire to avoid or postpone surgery.

review_status: AI draft - scientific, clinical, and editorial review required
content: Surgery is considered for symptomatic POP refractory to conservative care or when quality of life is significantly impaired. Procedures aim to restore normal pelvic anatomy and function, such as vaginal or abdominal hysterectomy with vault suspension, anterior or posterior colporrhaphy, sacrocolpopexy, or mesh-supported repairs. Choice of surgery depends on organ involvement, severity, patient age, comorbidities, and preferences. Surgical risks include recurrence, mesh complications, infection, and urinary or bowel dysfunction. Informed shared decision-making is paramount.

content: Preventing POP involves minimizing known risk factors: maintaining healthy body weight, practicing PFMT before and after childbirth, avoiding prolonged heavy lifting, managing chronic cough and constipation promptly, and considering estrogen replacement therapy during menopause where appropriate. Good posture and ergonomics during physical activities also reduce pelvic floor strain. Antepartum and postpartum pelvic floor rehabilitation can promote recovery from childbirth-related injury. These measures help preserve pelvic floor integrity and reduce prolapse risk or severity.

chunk_title: Misconceptions and Myths About Pelvic Organ Prolapse
content: Common misconceptions include the belief that all prolapses require surgical repair; in reality, many cases are mild and manageable conservatively. Some women fear POP is life-threatening—while it significantly affects quality of life, it is not fatal. Another myth is that prolapse inevitably worsens without treatment; evidence shows many remain stable or improve with pelvic floor exercises. There is also misunderstanding about pessary use causing infections; with proper care and monitoring, pessaries are safe. Addressing such myths is critical for empowering women with accurate information.

content: Management safety considerations depend on the treatment modality. Conservative treatments like PFMT and pessaries have few risks when properly applied; however, pessaries require fitting and regular cleaning to prevent vaginal irritation or infection. Surgical treatments carry risks such as bleeding, infection, anesthesia complications, mesh erosion (if mesh used), and recurrence of prolapse. Comprehensive preoperative evaluation and postoperative follow-up minimize complications. Patients must communicate symptoms promptly. Awareness of these aspects ensures safer care and better outcomes.
